data.title: We're Hopeful That IZEA Worldwide (NASDAQ:IZEA) Will Use Its Cash Wisely
data.description:
There's no doubt that money can be made by owning shares of unprofitable businesses. For example, biotech and mining exploration companies often lose money for years before finding success with a new treatment or mineral discovery. But while the successes are well known, investors should not ignore the very many unprofitable companies that simply burn through all their cash and collapse.

So should IZEA Worldwide (NASDAQ:IZEA) shareholders be worried about its cash burn? For the purposes of this article, cash burn is the annual rate at which an unprofitable company spends cash to fund its growth; its negative free cash flow. First, we'll determine its cash runway by comparing its cash burn with its cash reserves.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

When Might IZEA Worldwide Run Out Of Money?

A company's cash runway is the amount of time it would take to burn through its cash reserves at its current cash burn rate. As at June 2026, IZEA Worldwide had cash of US$47m and no debt. In the last year, its cash burn was US$2.6m. That means it had a cash runway of very many years as of June 2026. Even though this is but one measure of the company's cash burn, the thought of such a long cash runway warms our bellies in a comforting way. The image below shows how its cash balance has been changing over the last few years.

See our latest analysis for IZEA Worldwide

How Well Is IZEA Worldwide Growing?

Notably, IZEA Worldwide actually ramped up its cash burn very hard and fast in the last year, by 127%, signifying heavy investment in the business. While that's concerning on it's own, the fact that operating revenue was actually down 27% over the same period makes us positively tremulous. In light of the above-mentioned, we're pretty wary of the trajectory the company seems to be on. In reality, this article only makes a short study of the company's growth data. You can take a look at how IZEA Worldwide has developed its business over time by checking this visualization of its revenue and earnings history.

How Hard Would It Be For IZEA Worldwide To Raise More Cash For Growth?

While IZEA Worldwide seems to be in a fairly good position, it's still worth considering how easily it could raise more cash, even just to fuel faster growth. Companies can raise capital through either debt or equity. Commonly, a business will sell new shares in itself to raise cash and drive growth. We can compare a company's cash burn to its market capitalisation to get a sense for how many new shares a company would have to issue to fund one year's operations.

IZEA Worldwide's cash burn of US$2.6m is about 6.8% of its US$38m market capitalisation. That's a low proportion, so we figure the company would be able to raise more cash to fund growth, with a little dilution, or even to simply borrow some money.

So, Should We Worry About IZEA Worldwide's Cash Burn?

On this analysis of IZEA Worldwide's cash burn, we think its cash runway was reassuring, while its increasing cash burn has us a bit worried. While we're the kind of investors who are always a bit concerned about the risks involved with cash burning companies, the metrics we have discussed in this article leave us relatively comfortable about IZEA Worldwide's situation. On another note, IZEA Worldwide has 2 warning signs (and 1 which is concerning) we think you should know about.

data.title: Is Talen Energy (TLN) Undervalued Following Its Long Term Capacity Sales Deals?
data.description:
Capacity deals push Talen Energy toward more predictable earnings

Talen Energy (TLN) has kicked off a multi year reset of its cash flow profile, signing long dated capacity agreements that lock in revenue from key PJM power plants.

The centerpiece is a seven year sale of 750 megawatts of accredited capacity from the Guernsey Power Station to an investment grade buyer, expected to generate about US$100 million a year from 2029/2030 through 2035/2036.

Layered on top of earlier PJM auction clears, these commitments give Talen Energy roughly ten years and around US$1b of cumulative capacity revenue visibility tied to this slice of its fleet.

Management now has more than one third of its ELCC accredited capacity under long term contract, which lifts the contracted share of gross margin to 40% through 2036 and reduces earnings volatility.

The Guernsey deal is not the only piece in play. Talen Energy has also lined up separate agreements for the remaining 588 megawatts of Guernsey capacity in the 2029/2030 PJM delivery year and 702 megawatts from the Waterford Energy Center for three years through 2031/2032.

Those additional commitments push total contracted capacity from this transaction set to more than two gigawatts in the 2029/2030 planning year and 1.45 gigawatts in each of 2030/2031 and 2031/2032.

Talen Energy’s latest capacity deals come after a strong run in the shares, with a 7 day share price return of 11.04% and a 3 year total shareholder return of almost 7x. This is despite the year to date share price return being down 5.22% and the 1 day move slipping 2.76% to US$376.01 as investors digest earnings guidance, recent quarterly results and this new push toward more contracted cash flows.

Talen Energy closed at $376.01, while the leading valuation narrative pegs fair value at $395, suggesting a small undervaluation gap that depends heavily on future cash generation. According to Andrei_Niculescu, a Simply Wall St Community investor who wrote the narrative, the key question is whether current guidance on free cash flow holds up against leverage and PJM market risk.

That is attractive, if you underwrite the 2027 Adj FCF midpoint and apply a mid-to-high single-digit FCF yield after leverage. It is not attractive if you capitalize peak GAAP quarters or ignore that part of next year's capacity cash has already been sold forward.

Still, two pressure points could upset the Talen Energy story: a cut to the 2027 free cash flow guidance and any harsh redesign of PJM capacity rules.

The DCF story is one thing. On simple sales-based pricing, Talen Energy looks expensive, trading on a P/S of 3.7x against 2.5x for the wider North American renewable group and 1.7x for peers, even though the fair ratio model points to 4.2x as a level the market could move toward.
